text: 12 Lecture 12 12.1 Commuting operators Theorem 12.1. If A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ) are both diagonalizable. Then AB = BA if and only if there exists P ∈ Mn×n(F ) invertible such that P −1AP = diag(λ1, . . . , λn) and P −1BP = diag(µ1, . . . , µn). Proof. ⇐=: If P −1AP = diag(λ1, . . . , λn) and P −1BP = diag(µ1, . . . , µn), then AB = P diag(λ1µ1, . . . , λnµn)P −1 = BA. =⇒: Since A is diagonalizable over F , F n = E(λ1, A) ⊕ · · · ⊕ E(λm, A). If v ∈ E(λi, A) then A(Bv) = B(Av) = B(λiv) = λi(Bv) so Bv ∈ E(λi, A). Thus B(E(λi, A)) ⊂ E(λi, A) for any 1 ≤ i ≤ m. Thus if we let Q ∈ Mn×n(F ) such that its columns are basis of E(λi, A) for 1 ≤ i ≤ m, then Q −1AQ = diag(λ1, . . . , λn), Q −1BQ =      B1 0 · · · 0 0 B2 · · · 0 ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · Bm      where Bi ∈ Mki×ki(F ) for ki = dim E(λi, A). Since mB(B) = 0, we have mBi(x) | mB(x). Since B is diagonalizable, mB(x) has no repeated factors. Hence mBi(x) also has no repeated factors. Thus by Theorem 11.14 there exists a basis βi of E(λi, A) such that Bi is diagonalized. By Theorem 10.9, β = β1 ∪ · · · ∪ βm is a basis of F n. Since βi is a basis of E(λi, A), A is diagonalized under β. Since Bi is diagonalized under βi, B is diagonalized under β. If P is the change of basis matrix then P −1AP = diag(λ1, . . . , λn), P −1BP = diag(µ1, . . . , µn). Remark 12.2. The theorem is saying that there is a basis consisting of vectors that are eigenvectors of both A and B. This is not saying that any eigenvector of A is an eigenvector of B. We take A = ( 1 0 0 1 ) and B = ( 1 0 0 2 ) as an example. Clearly AB = BA and they are already in diagonalized under the standard basis e1, e2. However, since A = I, any nonzero vector is an eigenvectors of A but the eigenvectors of B are e1 with eigenvalue 1 and e2 with eigenvalue 2. Thus e1 + e2 is an eigenvector of A but not an eigenvector of B. Remark 12.3. Theorem 12.1 also appears in quantum mechanics. If the operators cor- responding to two physical quantities commute, then their values can be measured si- multaneously. If they do not commute, the famous uncertainty principle states that their values cannot be simultaneously determined. In fact, the uncertainty princi- ple has a qualitative version: we fix ψ ∈ Cn. For any A ∈ Mn×n(C), we write 70 ⟨A⟩ = ¯ψtAψ ∈ C. Let A, B ∈ Mn×n(C) with ¯At = A and ¯Bt = B. Then we have |(A − ⟨A⟩)2ψ|2|(B − ⟨B⟩)2ψ|2 ≥ | 1 2i ⟨[A, B]⟩|2. The term |(A − ⟨A⟩)2ψ|2 represents the variance of A in state ψ and the inequality is saying the product of variance is bounded below by the mean of the commutator so that if the commutator isn’t 0, then lowering the variance of A will increase the variance of B. 12.2 A brief introduction to Jordan canonical form In Lecture 9, we raised the question: given T : V → V a linear transformation, can we find a basis β such that [T ] β β is diagonal? We have seen in Example 9.27 and 11.12 that there are matrices that cannot be diagonalized. So we step back and ask what is the simplest form that [T ]β β can take? In Theorem 11.7, we see that we could make [T ] β β an upper triangular matrix. However, the issue with Theorem 11.7 is we have no information about the entries that are above the diagonal. The following theorem is the ultimate resolution to the question above. Theorem 12.4. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) be such that pA(x) splits in F . Then there exists P ∈ Mn×n(F ) invertible such that P −1AP =      Jk1(λ1) 0 · · · 0 0 Jk2(λ2) · · · 0 ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · Jkm(λm)      where Jki(λi) is a Jordan block. This is called the Jordan canonical form of A. Moreover, The Jordan canonical form for A unique up to a permutation of the Jordan blocks along the diagonal. Remark 12.5. The λi here need not be distinct. E.g. we could have a Jordan canonical form like     λ 1 0 0 0 λ 0 0 0 0 λ 1 0 0 0 λ     . Remark 12.6. In Example 11.12, we see that a Jordan block is diagonalizable if and only if it is 1 × 1. In general, A is diagonalizable if and only if all its Jordan block are 1 × 1, i.e. its Jordan canonical form is diagonal. Moreover, two matrices with different Jordan canonical form are not similar to each other. So we have: Theorem 12.7. A, B are similar if and only if their Jordan canonical form are the same up to permutation. The two theorems above are among the most difficult results to prove in linear algebra, and we unfortunately do not have time to cover their proofs in class. There are several different approaches in the literature, and I personally prefer the following two. 71 The first proof, from [1, Chapter 9], is completely elementary, and anyone with the background provided in these lecture notes should be able to follow it. The second proof, from [2, Chapter 12], is based on the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID. I find the first proof more accessible for students encountering these ideas for the first time, while the second presents linear algebra from a more advanced, conceptual viewpoint and connects naturally with the broader theory underlying the Jordan canonical form. In this note, we prove the simpler case for 2 × 2 matrices. Theorem 12.8 (Jordan canonical form for 2 × 2 matrices). Let A ∈ M2×2(F ) be such that pA(x) splits in F . Then there exists P ∈ M2×2(F ) invertible such that either P −1AP = ( λ1 0 0 λ2 ) or P −1AP = ( λ 1 0 λ ). Proof. If A has two distinct eigenvalues then A is diagonalizable by Corollary 10.12. If A has one eigenvalue and dim E(λ, A) = 2, then A = λI is diagonalizable. If A has one eigenvalue and dim E(λ, A) = 1, then by rank-nullity Theorem 4.14, rank(λI − A) = 1. Let 0 ̸= v ∈ im(A − λI). Then v = (A − λI)w for 0 ̸= w ∈ F 2 i.e. Aw = λw + v. The characteristic polynomial of A is (x − λ)2. Then by Cayley-Hamilton theorem, (A − λI)2 = 0. Then we have (A − λI)v = (A − λI)2w = 0 i.e. Av = λv. We claim that v, w are linearly independent. If av + bw = 0, then applying (A − λI) on both sides 0 = (A − λI)(av + bw) = bv. Since v ̸= 0, we have b = 0. Thus av = 0 and hence a = 0. Thus v, w are linearly independent. We let P = (v, w). Then P is invertible, and P −1AP = ( λ 1 0 λ ) The proof provides a good way to compute the Jordan canonical form for 2 × 2 matrices Example 12.9. We recall Example 9.27 where A = ( −1 −4 1 3 ) and pA(x) = (x − 1)2. Then λ = 1 is the only eigenvalue of A. Since A−I = ( −2 −4 1 2 ) , dim ker(A−I) = 1 < 2. im(A − I) = span ( −2 1 ). Let v = (−2 1 ). Solving (A − I)w = ( −2 1 ) , we get w = ( 1 0 ) . We set P = ( −2 1 1 0 ) , then we have P −1AP = (1 1 0 1 ) . We have seen in Example 9.23 that a real matrix can have eigenvalues not in R. Of course we can view it as a complex matrix and apply Theorem 12.8. However, we would like to know what is the simplest form of it under similarity by P ∈ M2×2(R) invertible. Theorem 12.10 (Real canonical form for 2 × 2 matrices over R). Let A ∈ M2×2(R). Then there exists P ∈ M2×2(R) invertible such that either P −1AP = (λ1 0 0 λ2 ) or P −1AP = ( λ 1 0 λ ) or P −1AP = ( a b −b a ) where a ± bi are the eigenvalues of A in C. 72 Proof. If pA(x) splits in R, then the theorem follows from Theorem 12.8. We deal with the case where A has no real eigenvalues. Then pA(x) = x2 − tr(A)x + det(A) has complex roots a ± bi for b ̸= 0. Let v ∈ C2 be an eigenvector with eigenvalue a + bi. Then Av = (a + bi)v. Let v = v1 + v2i where v1 = Re v ∈ R2 and v2 = Im v ∈ R2. We write P = (v1, v2) ∈ M2×2(R). Then Av1 + Av2i = A(v1 + v2i) = (a + bi)(v1 + v2i) = (av1 − bv2) + (av2 + bv1)i. Thus Av1 = av1 − bv2 and Av2 = av2 + bv1. Then P −1AP = ( a b −b a ) provided P is invertible which can be seen as follows: By Remark 9.25 , v, ¯v are the eigenvector with distinct eigenvalues a + bi and a − bi. Thus by Theorem 10.9 v and ¯v are linearly independent. That v1, v2 are linearly independent follows from the following lemma. Lemma 12.11. Let v ∈ Cn. If v, ¯v are linearly independent, then Re v and Im v are linearly independent. Proof. We have Re v = 1 2 (v + ¯v) and Im v = 1 2i (v − ¯v). Suppose a Re v + b Im v = 0 for a, b ∈ C. Then ( 1 2 a + 1 2i b)v + ( 1 2 a − 1 2i b)¯v = 0. Since v, ¯v are linearly independent, we have ( 1 2 1 2i 1 2 − 1 2i ) ( a b ) = ( 0 0 ) . Since det ( 1 2 1 2i 1 2 − 1 2i ) = − 1 2i ̸= 0, we have a = b = 0. Example 12.12. We recall Example 9.24 where A = ( −1 2 −1 1 ) ∈ M2×2(C) and pA(x) = x2 + 1 = (x − i)(x + i). We have v1 = ( 1 − i 1 ) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue i. Then Re v1 = ( 1 1 ) and Im v1 = ( −1 0 ). If P = ( 1 −1 1 0 ) then P −1AP = ( 0 1 −1 0 ) . 12.3 Convergence of a sequence of matrices Definition 12.13. A sequence of matrices {Ak = (a (k) ij )} ⊂ Mm×n(C) converges to a matrix A = (aij) ∈ Mm×n(C) if a(k) ij → aij for any i = 1, . . . , m, j = 1, . . . , n as k → ∞. We write lim k→∞ Ak = A. Definition 12.14. Let A(t) = (aij(t)) ∈ Mm×n(C) be a family of matrix depending on t ∈ (a, b). Then we define the derivative at t to be A′(t) = lim h→0 A(t + h) − A(t) h . Lemma 12.15. If A(t) = (aij(t)) where aij are differentiable at t then A′(t) = (a′ ij(t)). 73 Proof. Since a′ ij(t) = limh→0 aij (t+h)−aij (t) h exists, we have A′(t) exists and A′(t) = (a′ ij(t)). 12.4 Matrix function Definition 12.16.
